modules.title: Reading the Business
modules.summary: What the role is for, and how to find the real problem rather than the stated one.

lessons.title: What a Forward Deployed Engineer Is Actually For
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The gap the role exists to close

Software companies keep discovering the same uncomfortable fact: the product works in the demo and stalls in the customer's environment. Not because it is broken, but because the customer's data is shaped differently, their process has an undocumented step, and the person who has to use it every day was not in the room when it was bought.

A Forward Deployed Engineer is the person sent to close that gap. You sit inside the customer's business, find out what actually happens there, and make the product work in that reality — building whatever integration, transformation or glue the situation needs.

## What makes it different from consulting

A consultant delivers a project and leaves. You are accountable to two masters: the customer, who wants their problem solved, and your own product team, who need the solution to generalise. A bespoke thing that works for one customer and teaches the company nothing is a failure even when the customer is delighted.

That tension is the job. Every engagement, you are deciding what to build specially and what to push back into the product.

## What you are actually measured on

Not lines of code. Not even uptime. You are measured on whether the customer's workflow changed — whether the analyst who used to spend three hours on a task now spends twenty minutes and trusts the result.

This is worth internalising early, because it changes what you do on day one. An engineer optimises the system. A Forward Deployed Engineer optimises the user's Tuesday.

## Why the pay is what it is

The premium is not for the coding. It is for the willingness to sit in a room with a sceptical operations lead and stay there until you understand their job. Most strong engineers will not do this. That scarcity is the whole compensation story, and it is also why the role is unusually safe from automation.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Product Team] -->|ships a product| B[FDE]
  C[Customer Reality] -->|messy data, undocumented process| B
  B --> D[Working Deployment]
  B -->|generalised requirements| A
keyTakeaways: The role exists because products work in demos and stall in customer environments
You answer to the customer and to your own product team, and those goals conflict
Success is a changed user workflow, not a shipped feature
The premium is paid for the customer-facing half, which is the half most engineers avoid

questions.prompt: A customer's executive sponsor is delighted with a bespoke solution you built, but nothing you learned went back to the product team. How should this engagement be judged?
questions.explanation: A Forward Deployed Engineer serves two masters. A happy customer and zero product learning is half a job — the company paid field-engineering rates for a one-off.

options.text: A partial success at best — the customer is served but the company learned nothing that generalises
A complete success, because customer satisfaction is the only measure
A failure, because bespoke work is never justified
Neutral — product feedback is the product manager's responsibility

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes how a Forward Deployed Engineer's work is measured?
questions.explanation: The output is a changed workflow. Systems metrics matter only insofar as they serve it.

options.text: Whether the user's day-to-day workflow measurably changed
Volume of code shipped during the engagement
Number of integrations built
Uptime of the deployed service

lessons.title: Discovery That Finds the Real Problem
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The stated problem is rarely the problem

The sponsor who signed the contract will tell you what they think is wrong. They are describing the problem from two levels up, filtered through what they believe software can do. The operators three levels down have a different account, and theirs is usually closer to the truth.

Both are data. Neither is the answer.

## Watch the work, do not ask about it

The single highest-value hour of any engagement is sitting behind someone while they do the task. Not a meeting about the task — the task itself.

You will see things nobody would have told you: the spreadsheet they keep on the side because the system is too slow, the field they fill with a sentinel value because it is required and they do not have it, the colleague they message to check something the system should have told them.

Those workarounds are the map. Each one marks a place where the official process and the real process have diverged, and that divergence is where value lives.

## Questions that work

Ask for specifics and history, not opinions:

- *"Walk me through the last time you did this. Not the usual case — the last one."*
- *"What do you do when the data is wrong?"*
- *"What happens if you just don't do this step?"*
- *"Who chases you when this is late, and what do they say?"*
- *"What did you try before, and why did it stop?"*

The last one matters more than it looks. Almost every process you meet has a graveyard of previous attempts, and the reasons they died are the constraints nobody will state directly.

## Write it down where they can see it

End discovery by writing the workflow back to them, in their words, and asking what you got wrong. Being corrected is the point. A customer who corrects your draft has started collaborating; one who nods at your summary has not read it.
lessons.codeExample:
Discovery log — Renewals team, day 2

OBSERVED (sat with M., renewals analyst, 90 min)
  09:10  Opens CRM, filters renewals in next 90 days -> 47 accounts
  09:18  Copies account list into a personal spreadsheet
         ^ WORKAROUND: CRM export is "too slow and drops the usage column"
  09:25  For each account, opens the usage dashboard in a second tab
  09:40  Opens contract PDF from a shared drive, Ctrl-F for "auto-renew"
         ^ WORKAROUND: no link from CRM to the contract; finds it by customer name
  10:15  Messages Legal to confirm a notice period
         ^ WORKAROUND: contract language is ambiguous; this happens ~3x/week
  10:30  Has reviewed 6 of 47 accounts

STATED BY SPONSOR (VP Revenue)
  "We need AI to predict churn."

STATED BY OPERATOR (M.)
  "I don't need a prediction. I need to stop opening four systems per account."

CONSTRAINT FOUND (not volunteered)
  Previous churn-scoring tool was abandoned in 2024 — M.: "it gave us a number
  with no reason attached, so nobody trusted it." Any score we produce must
  show its evidence.

OPEN QUESTION FOR TOMORROW
  What happens today when the usage data and the contract disagree?
keyTakeaways: The sponsor's problem and the operator's problem are different; collect both
Watch the task being done rather than asking about it — workarounds are the map
Ask about the last specific instance, not the general case
Ask what was tried before; the graveyard holds the unstated constraints
Write the workflow back and invite correction

questions.prompt: During discovery you notice an analyst maintains a private spreadsheet alongside the official system. What is the most useful interpretation?
questions.explanation: A workaround is evidence that the official process diverged from the real one. That gap is where the value is.

options.text: A signal that the official system fails them somewhere worth investigating
A training problem to be corrected
A data-governance violation to escalate
Noise — personal preference, not a system issue

questions.prompt: Which discovery questions tend to surface unstated constraints?
questions.explanation: Specific past instances and previous failed attempts reveal constraints nobody will volunteer. Hypotheticals invite speculation.

options.text: Walk me through the last time you did this
What did you try before, and why did it stop?
What do you do when the data is wrong?
If you could have anything, what would the ideal system look like?

modules.title: Scoping and Saying No
modules.summary: Turning what you found into a deliverable both sides can be held to, and handling the politics that decide whether it gets used.

lessons.title: From Ambiguity to a Scoped Deliverable
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Scope is a promise about what you will not do

Most failed deployments were scoped as a list of features. Feature lists have no edges: every conversation adds one, and by week six the deliverable has quietly doubled while the date has not moved.

Scope well and you write down three things: the outcome, the measure, and the exclusions. The exclusions are the part people skip and the part that saves the engagement.

## Write the success measure first

Before anything else, agree the sentence that will be true if this worked. Not "improve the renewal process" — something countable:

> *An analyst can complete a renewal review in under 20 minutes, from a starting list of at-risk accounts, without opening the contract drive.*

Now you have an edge. Anything that serves that sentence is in scope. Anything that does not is a conversation, and you are having it in week one rather than week six.

## Name the exclusions out loud

Write them into the same document:

> *Not in scope: predicting churn probability; changes to the CRM; anything touching the billing system; mobile access.*

This feels confrontational the first time. It is the opposite — it is the thing that lets you say yes enthusiastically to everything that is in.

## Size against the riskiest unknown

The schedule risk is almost never the part you understand. It is the source system nobody can describe, the security review of unknown length, the data-access approval that has to go through a committee.

Find those in week one and put them first. An engagement that discovers an eight-week security review in week seven is over.

## Re-scope openly when you learn something

Discovery continues after discovery ends. When week three teaches you the original measure was wrong, say so immediately and propose the new one. Customers forgive a changed plan explained early. They do not forgive a plan that was quietly wrong for a month.
lessons.codeExample:
# Engagement scope — Renewals Copilot (2 weeks)

## Success measure
An analyst completes a renewal review in under 20 minutes, starting from a
ranked at-risk list, without opening the contract drive.
Baseline measured on day 1: 28 minutes median across 6 observed reviews.

## In scope
- Ranked at-risk account list, refreshed nightly
- Contract clause lookup with the clause quoted inline
- Usage summary per account, joined from the existing warehouse extract

## Explicitly NOT in scope
- Churn probability prediction        (previous attempt failed on trust; needs its own engagement)
- Any write-back into the CRM         (requires a change-control board we cannot reach in 2 weeks)
- Billing system integration
- Mobile access

## Riskiest unknowns — resolve in week 1
1. Read access to the contract drive          owner: IT Security   status: REQUESTED day 1
2. Schema of the nightly warehouse extract    owner: Data team     status: UNKNOWN
3. Whether contract PDFs are text or scanned  owner: us            status: sampling today

## Agreed review points
Day 3  — walkthrough of the ranked list with M. and one other analyst
Day 7  — working prototype, scope re-confirmed or renegotiated in writing
Day 14 — handover and measurement against the baseline
keyTakeaways: Scope is defined by exclusions as much as inclusions — write both down
Agree a countable success sentence before agreeing any feature
Schedule risk lives in the unknowns: approvals, access, undocumented systems. Front-load them
Re-scope out loud the moment you learn the plan was wrong

questions.prompt: Why are explicit exclusions considered the most valuable part of a scope document?
questions.explanation: Inclusions expand silently under pressure. A written exclusion turns each addition into a deliberate, dated conversation rather than quiet scope creep.

options.text: They make every addition an explicit conversation rather than silent creep
They reduce the customer's expectations of quality
They shift legal liability onto the customer
They shorten the scope document

questions.prompt: You have two weeks. One task is a well-understood data transformation; the other depends on a security approval of unknown duration. What do you sequence first?
questions.explanation: Unknowns are where schedule risk lives. Discovering an eight-week approval in week seven ends the engagement; discovering it in week one lets you re-plan.

options.text: The security approval, because unknown duration is the real schedule risk
The transformation, to show early progress
Both in parallel at half speed
Whichever the sponsor considers more visible

lessons.title: The Politics of a Deployment
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The sponsor is not the user

The person who bought the software and the person who must use it are rarely the same, and their incentives can be opposed. The sponsor wants a visible win. The user wants their day not to get worse. A deployment that delights the first and irritates the second dies quietly about a month after you leave.

You need both. Practically, that means spending your political capital on the sponsor and your hours on the users.

## Find out what the tool threatens

Every tool that automates part of a job implies something about the person doing that job. Sometimes that implication is fine. Sometimes the analyst you are sitting with is reasonably wondering whether they are training their replacement.

Pretending this is not happening is the worst available option. Say plainly what the tool does and does not do, and mean it. If the honest answer is that the role changes, say that too — people can handle an uncomfortable truth far better than a cheerful evasion they do not believe.

## Recruit one operator early

Find the person who is respected by their peers, is a bit frustrated with the current process, and is willing to tell you when something is wrong. Give them the prototype before it is good. Credit them in the demo.

That person is worth more than the sponsor's enthusiasm, because they are who everyone else will ask.

## Identify the quiet blocker

There is usually someone whose cooperation you need and whose objection has not been raised in a meeting: the data owner who is not convinced, the security lead who was told rather than asked, the team lead whose process you are changing.

Go and see them before you need something from them. The meeting costs half an hour in week one and can cost three weeks in week five.

## Leave the credit behind

The engagement ends. What persists is whether the customer's own people feel the thing is theirs. Put their names on it, teach them to change it, and let them present it. Your win is that it is still running in six months.
keyTakeaways: The sponsor and the user have different incentives; you need both
Be direct about what the tool means for people's roles — evasion is transparent
Recruit one respected operator early and let them shape it
Meet the quiet blocker in week one, before you need anything
Hand over the credit; longevity depends on ownership

questions.prompt: An operator asks, half-joking, whether your tool is going to eliminate their job. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: People read evasion accurately and it costs you the cooperation you need. An honest answer, including an uncomfortable one, is both more ethical and more effective.

options.text: Answer plainly what the tool does and does not change, including if the role does change
Reassure them it definitely will not, to keep the engagement moving
Redirect the question to their manager
Avoid the topic; it is outside your remit

questions.prompt: Who is most valuable to recruit early in a deployment?
questions.explanation: Peers ask the respected, slightly frustrated operator what they think. Their verdict travels further than the sponsor's enthusiasm.

options.text: A respected operator who is frustrated with the current process and will tell you when something is wrong
The most senior executive available
The most technically capable person in IT
Whoever is most enthusiastic in the kickoff meeting

modules.title: Prototyping in the Room
modules.summary: Building something real inside a week, and showing it to the people whose opinion decides whether it survives.

lessons.title: The One-Week Proof of Concept
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The point of a prototype is to be wrong quickly

A proof of concept exists to convert an argument into an observation. Until someone uses it, everything you both believe about the workflow is a hypothesis.

So build the smallest thing that can be wrong in a useful way, and get it in front of a real user with real-shaped data inside a week.

## Real-shaped data or nothing

A prototype on clean invented data proves nothing, because every hard problem in the deployment lives in the dirt: the duplicate customer records, the three date formats, the accounts with no usage history at all.

If you cannot get the real data yet — and often you cannot, for good reasons — generate synthetic data that reproduces the *defects* you observed, not just the schema. A generator that only produces well-formed rows is a generator that hides your problems until week four.

## Build the spine, fake the limbs

Make one path work completely, end to end, and stub everything else visibly. A user can react to one real path. They cannot react to five half-paths, and neither can you.

Stub with something obviously fake — a labelled placeholder — rather than something plausible. A plausible stub gets mistaken for working software and you will be asked why it broke.

## Keep the seam where production will need it

The one piece of engineering discipline worth paying for in a prototype: keep the business logic separate from the transport and the model call. Pure functions in the middle, integrations at the edges.

This costs an hour and is the difference between a prototype that extends into production and one that must be thrown away. It also means you can test the logic without a network call, which you will want by day three.

## Timebox and demo on the day you said

Demo on the agreed day even if it is not ready. A prototype shown late and polished teaches you less than one shown on time and rough, and the date you keep is itself evidence about how the rest of the engagement will go.
lessons.codeExample:
# generate_data.py — synthetic customers that reproduce the defects we OBSERVED,
# not an idealised schema. Every problem below was seen in the real extract.
import json, random
from datetime import date, timedelta

random.seed(42)  # reproducible: the same dataset gives the same risk ranking

REGIONS = ["EMEA", "NA", "APAC"]

def make(i):
    row = {
        "customer_id": f"CUST-{i:04d}",
        "name": f"Customer {i}",
        "region": random.choice(REGIONS),
        "arr": round(random.uniform(10_000, 500_000), 2),
        "renewal_date": (date.today() + timedelta(days=random.randint(-30, 180))).isoformat(),
        "logins_last_30d": random.randint(0, 400),
        "open_tickets": random.randint(0, 12),
    }

    # --- observed defect 1: ~8% of accounts have no usage history at all.
    # The first prototype silently scored these as "zero usage = high risk",
    # which was wrong: they are new accounts, not dying ones.
    if random.random() < 0.08:
        row["logins_last_30d"] = None

    # --- observed defect 2: three date formats in the live extract.
    if random.random() < 0.15:
        y, m, d = row["renewal_date"].split("-")
        row["renewal_date"] = f"{d}/{m}/{y}"

    # --- observed defect 3: duplicate customer_id with differing ARR.
    # Discovered on day 2; the warehouse join fans out on these.
    return row

rows = [make(i) for i in range(1, 51)]
rows.append({**rows[7], "arr": rows[7]["arr"] * 1.2})  # the duplicate

json.dump(rows, open("data/customers.json", "w"), indent=2)
print(f"wrote {len(rows)} rows, including {sum(1 for r in rows if r['logins_last_30d'] is None)} "
      f"with no usage history and 1 duplicate id")
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Observed defects in discovery] --> B[Synthetic generator]
  B --> C[Prototype]
  C --> D[Real user, real reaction]
  D -->|corrections| A
  C -.->|pure logic kept separate| E[Extends into production]
keyTakeaways: A prototype exists to be wrong quickly in front of a real user
Synthetic data must reproduce the observed defects, not just the schema
Make one path work completely; stub the rest visibly rather than plausibly
Keep business logic in pure functions from day one — it costs an hour and saves the rewrite
Demo on the agreed date even when it is rough

questions.prompt: Why should synthetic prototype data reproduce the defects you observed rather than only the schema?
questions.explanation: The hard problems live in the dirt. Clean synthetic data postpones every real difficulty until production, when it is expensive.

options.text: Because the hard problems are in the dirty data, and clean data hides them until late
Because it makes the dataset larger
Because customers expect realistic-looking demos
Because defective data trains better models

questions.prompt: Which is the better way to stub an unfinished part of a prototype?
questions.explanation: A plausible stub gets mistaken for working software; you then get asked why it broke. An obviously fake placeholder keeps the conversation honest.

options.text: An obviously labelled placeholder
Plausible hard-coded output that looks real
An empty screen with no explanation
An error message

lessons.title: Demoing to People Who Will Have to Use It
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Demo the workflow, not the software

The instinct is to show what you built: here is the API, here is the pipeline, here is the clever bit. Resist it. Open with the user's task and complete it in front of them.

> *"M., this is the review you did on Tuesday that took twenty-eight minutes. Let's do it again."*

Then do it. Everything you built is visible in passing, and now it is in a frame where the audience can judge it.

## Use their data and their vocabulary

Their account names. Their region codes. The words they use for their own process — if they say "notice window" and your UI says "termination period", change the UI.

This sounds cosmetic. It is not: the moment a user sees their own world represented accurately, they start critiquing the substance instead of the surface. That critique is what the demo is for.

## Show a failure on purpose

Include one case where the tool does not know the answer, and show it saying so. This is the single most trust-building thing you can do, especially with a group that has been burned by a previous tool that produced confident nonsense.

A tool that admits uncertainty gets believed when it does not.

## Leave silence

Ask "what's wrong with this?" and then stop talking. Count to ten if you have to. The first answer is politeness; the second answer, which only arrives if you wait, is the useful one.

## Write down the objections verbatim

Not your paraphrase — their words. Read them back at the end and confirm. Half of them will turn out to be the same underlying issue, and finding that is often the most valuable output of the session.

## Close with what happens next and when

End every demo with a date and a named owner for each action. A demo that ends in general enthusiasm produces nothing; one that ends with three dated commitments produces three things.
keyTakeaways: Open with the user's task and complete it, rather than touring the architecture
Use their data and their vocabulary; it moves critique from surface to substance
Deliberately show the tool admitting it does not know — it is the strongest trust signal
Ask what is wrong and then be silent; the second answer is the real one
Record objections verbatim and close with dated, owned actions

questions.prompt: Why deliberately include a case where the tool cannot answer?
questions.explanation: A tool that visibly admits uncertainty earns belief for the cases where it is confident, especially with users burned by a previous tool that bluffed.

options.text: It earns trust for the answers the tool does give
It lowers expectations so later problems are forgiven
It demonstrates technical depth
It fills demo time

questions.prompt: You ask a group what is wrong with the prototype and get a polite, minor comment. What should you do?
questions.explanation: The first answer is politeness. Silence is uncomfortable enough that someone fills it with the real objection.

options.text: Stay silent and wait; the second answer is usually the substantive one
Move on, since no serious objection was raised
Defend the design decision they questioned
Ask the sponsor for their view instead

title: Phase 2 — Integration & Deployment in Someone Else's Environment
summary: The engineering that deployments actually fail on: source systems you cannot change, data you are not allowed to copy, an environment you did not build, and an operations team who will own it after you leave.
outcomes: Integrate against a source system whose owner will not change anything for you
Make ingestion idempotent and prove what landed with a reconciliation report
Work inside data residency and PII constraints rather than around them
Deploy into an environment with rules you did not set
Hand over to an operations team so the system survives your departure

modules.title: Systems You Do Not Control
modules.summary: Ingesting from sources that are inconsistent, undocumented and not going to change.

lessons.title: Integrating Against an Unwilling Source
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Assume nothing will be fixed for you

The source system belongs to a team with their own roadmap, and your engagement is not on it. The export will keep having three date formats. The customer ID will keep not being unique. Nobody is going to add the field you need.

Design from that assumption and you build something that works. Design from a promised fix and you build something that works in the demo.

## Find the contract that actually exists

Before writing a connector, establish four things and write them down:

1. **Cardinality** — is the key actually unique? Check, do not ask. Count distinct against count.
2. **Volume and growth** — how many rows today, how many next year.
3. **Freshness** — when is it written, and is it complete at the moment you read it? A nightly job you read at 02:00 may be half-written.
4. **Failure mode** — what does the source do when *it* fails? Silence, a partial file, and a zero-row file are three very different problems and you must tell them apart.

The fourth is the one people skip and the one that causes the 3 a.m. call.

## Zero rows is not the same as no file

A source that produces an empty export because the upstream job failed will, in a naive pipeline, look exactly like a day with no activity. Your system will happily write "no at-risk accounts today" and be believed.

Treat a suspiciously empty load as a failure requiring a decision, not a normal result.

## Isolate the mess at the boundary

Put every source-specific quirk in one layer, and let nothing past it. Downstream code should never contain a comment about how this particular customer formats dates.

That boundary is also what makes the second customer cheap. If parsing quirks are scattered through your business logic, every new deployment is a rewrite.

## Detect drift, do not absorb it

When a column appears, disappears or changes type, the pipeline should stop and say so. Silent absorption means the tool quietly stops using a field and nobody notices for a quarter.
lessons.codeExample:
-- Establish the contract that actually exists, before writing any connector.
-- Run these against the source. Do not accept verbal answers.

-- 1. Is the key actually unique? (It was not, in three of my last four engagements.)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS distinct_ids,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS duplicate_rows
FROM   source_customers;

-- 2. Which of these columns is actually populated? "Required" in a spec means nothing.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total,
       COUNT(renewal_date)      AS has_renewal_date,
       COUNT(usage_last_30d)    AS has_usage,
       COUNT(contract_ref)      AS has_contract_ref
FROM   source_customers;

-- 3. Freshness: when was this data actually written, and is the window complete?
SELECT MIN(last_modified) AS oldest,
       MAX(last_modified) AS newest,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE last_modified >= CURRENT_DATE) AS written_today
FROM   source_customers;

-- 4. Distribution, so a "suspiciously empty" load can be defined numerically
--    rather than by feel. Anything below ~60% of the trailing median is a stop.
SELECT load_date, COUNT(*) AS rows_loaded
FROM   ingest_audit
GROUP  BY load_date
ORDER  BY load_date DESC
LIMIT  30;
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR A[Source you cannot change] --> B[Boundary layer
all quirks live here] B --> C{Drift check} C -->|changed| D[Halt + report] C -->|ok| E{Volume sane?} E -->|suspiciously empty| D E -->|ok| F[Clean domain model] F --> G[Business logic
knows nothing about the source]
keyTakeaways: Assume the source will never be fixed for you, and design accordingly
Verify key uniqueness, volume, freshness and failure mode before writing a connector
An empty load and a quiet day look identical — treat suspicious emptiness as a failure
Confine every source quirk to one boundary layer; downstream code stays clean
Schema drift must halt and report, never be silently absorbed

questions.prompt: A nightly export arrives with zero rows. Why is this dangerous to treat as a normal result?
questions.explanation: Zero rows from a failed upstream job is indistinguishable from a genuinely quiet day. The system will publish a confident, wrong answer.

options.text: A failed upstream job and a genuinely quiet day are indistinguishable, so a wrong answer gets published confidently
Empty files waste storage
It will cause a divide-by-zero in the aggregation
It is not dangerous; zero rows means no work to do

questions.prompt: What should happen when a source column changes type between loads?
questions.explanation: Silent absorption means a field quietly stops being used and nobody notices for a quarter. Drift must be loud.

options.text: The load halts and reports the drift before writing anything
The value is coerced to the expected type and loading continues
The column is dropped and loading continues
A warning is logged and loading continues

lessons.title: Idempotency, Reconciliation and Proving the Data Landed
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Everything runs twice eventually

A network blip, a retried job, an operator who clicks the button again because nothing seemed to happen. Your ingest will run twice on the same input, and the only question is whether that is harmless.

Make it harmless. Upsert on a natural key rather than inserting, so the same export applied twice leaves exactly the same state as applying it once.

## Reject loudly, keep the evidence

Rows will fail validation. The temptation is to log and skip; the consequence is a number that is quietly wrong and unexplainable three weeks later when someone asks why their account is missing.

Write rejected rows to a table with the reason. Two things follow: you can answer "where is my account?" in thirty seconds, and the rejection rate becomes a metric you can alert on.

## The three numbers must agree

Every load produces a reconciliation record: rows read, rows accepted, rows rejected. If read does not equal accepted plus rejected, something is being lost silently and you have a bug, not a report.

This sounds trivially obvious. It is also the check that catches most pipeline defects, because almost every silent-loss bug breaks it.

## Make the report customer-facing

Write the reconciliation as something you could send to the customer without editing. This constraint is doing real work: it forces reasons to be human-readable, and it means that when the customer asks whether the data is right, you send a report instead of starting an investigation.

## Retry with limits, then stop

Transient failures deserve a retry with backoff. Permanent ones deserve a clear failure. A pipeline that retries forever is a pipeline that hangs, and a hung pipeline gets noticed much later than a failed one.
lessons.codeExample:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class LoadResult:
    """The three numbers that must agree. If they don't, we have a bug, not a report."""
    read: int = 0
    accepted: int = 0
    rejected: list = field(default_factory=list)   # (natural_key, reason)

    def balances(self) -> bool:
        return self.read == self.accepted + len(self.rejected)


def load(rows, conn) -> LoadResult:
    result = LoadResult()

    for row in rows:
        result.read += 1

        problem = validate(row)
        if problem:
            # Kept, not dropped. "Where is my account?" is now a 30-second answer.
            conn.execute(
                "INSERT INTO ingest_rejected (natural_key, reason, payload, load_id) "
                "VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s)",
                (row.get("customer_id"), problem, json_dumps(row), conn.load_id))
            result.rejected.append((row.get("customer_id"), problem))
            continue

        # Idempotent: the same export applied twice leaves the same state as once.
        conn.execute(
            """INSERT INTO customer (customer_id, name, region, arr, renewal_date)
               VALUES (%(customer_id)s, %(name)s, %(region)s, %(arr)s, %(renewal_date)s)
               ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE SET
                 name          = EXCLUDED.name,
                 region        = EXCLUDED.region,
                 arr           = EXCLUDED.arr,
                 renewal_date  = EXCLUDED.renewal_date,
                 updated_at    = NOW()""", row)
        result.accepted += 1

    if not result.balances():
        # Never publish a report whose own arithmetic is wrong.
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"load does not balance: read={result.read} "
            f"accepted={result.accepted} rejected={len(result.rejected)}")

    return result
keyTakeaways: Every ingest runs twice eventually; upsert on a natural key so it is harmless
Retain rejected rows with reasons rather than logging and skipping
Read must equal accepted plus rejected — this check catches most silent-loss bugs
Write the reconciliation report to be sent to the customer unedited
Retry transient failures with backoff and a bound; never retry forever

questions.prompt: What does upserting on a natural key buy an ingestion pipeline?
questions.explanation: Retries, duplicate triggers and nervous operators all cause double runs. Upsert makes the second run a no-op instead of a duplication.

options.text: Running the same export twice leaves the same state as running it once
Faster inserts than a plain INSERT
Automatic schema migration
Guaranteed ordering of rows

questions.prompt: A load reports 1,000 rows read, 940 accepted and 40 rejected. What is the correct response?
questions.explanation: Read must equal accepted plus rejected. 940 + 40 = 980, so twenty rows vanished silently. That is a defect, not a reportable result.

options.text: Treat it as a bug — twenty rows were lost silently
Publish it; a 94% acceptance rate is healthy
Re-run the load and publish whichever result balances

modules.title: The Customer's Constraints
modules.summary: Data you may not copy, environments you did not build, and rules that are not negotiable.

lessons.title: Data Residency, PII and What You Cannot Copy
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Find the rules before you need them

Every regulated customer has constraints on where their data may live, who may see it and what may leave the building. These are usually discoverable on day one and catastrophic to discover in week five, after you have built a pipeline that copies everything into your own cloud account.

Ask early and specifically: *Which of this data may leave your network? Which region must it stay in? Who is allowed to see production records — am I?*

## Assume you are not allowed to see production data

Plan for the case where you cannot. It is common, it is reasonable, and it is entirely workable if you design for it: develop against synthetic data that mirrors the observed defects, and run against real data only inside their environment.

Engineers who have not worked this way find it constraining. Engineers who have find it clarifying — it forces the data contract to be explicit rather than discovered by looking.

## Minimise rather than mask

The safest personal data is the data you did not ingest. Before reaching for masking or tokenisation, ask whether you need the field at all. A renewal-risk model needs usage counts and contract terms; it does not need names, email addresses or phone numbers.

Dropping a column at the boundary is simpler, cheaper and more defensible than protecting it everywhere downstream.

## Watch what leaves in a prompt

This is the constraint that catches teams out. A model call hosted outside the customer's boundary is an egress of whatever is in the prompt — including the retrieved context the user never sees.

Establish before you build: which provider, in which region, with what retention, and what exactly may appear in a prompt. Log prompts in a way that lets you answer "what did we send?" later, and treat that log as sensitive because it is.

## Write it down and get it confirmed

Whatever you agree, restate it in writing and have their security contact confirm. Not for bureaucracy — because the person who told you verbally in week one will have moved teams by the audit.

flowchart TB subgraph Customer[Customer boundary] A[(Production data)] --> B[Ingest + minimise] B --> C[Business logic] C --> D[Deployed app] end subgraph Us[Our environment] E[(Synthetic data
same defects, no PII)] --> F[Development + tests] end C -.->|approved fields only
region + retention agreed| G[External model provider] F -.->|code, never data| D
keyTakeaways: Find residency, access and egress rules on day one; they are fatal to discover late
Plan to develop without production data access; synthetic data with real defects makes it workable
Minimise first — the field you never ingest needs no protection
A prompt to an external model is an egress, including its retrieved context
Restate agreed constraints in writing and get security to confirm

options.text: A field never ingested needs no protection anywhere downstream

lessons.title: Deploying Into an Environment You Did Not Build
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Their rules, not your preferences

You will meet a base image you must use, a registry you must push to, a network with no outbound access, a change window on Thursdays, and an approval step involving a person you have not met.

None of this is negotiable in the timeframe you have. Find it in week one, build to it, and stop wishing it were otherwise.

## Package so it runs anywhere

Containerise, and keep every environment-specific value in configuration rather than in the image. The same artifact should run on your laptop, in their staging environment and in their production, differing only by what is injected at start.

The test: can you point the container at a different database with an environment variable, and nothing else?

## Health and readiness are not the same

*Health* says the process is alive. *Readiness* says it can serve traffic — dependencies reachable, migrations applied, cache warm.

Conflating them means a deploy that routes traffic to an instance that is running but cannot answer, and the resulting five minutes of errors look exactly like an outage.

## No outbound network is normal

Many secure environments do not allow the container to reach the internet. That breaks anything that downloads at startup: package installs, model weights, remote configuration.

Bake it into the image or mount it. Discovering this during the deployment window is how one-hour deployments become three-day deployments.

## Rehearse the rollback before you need it

Deploy to their staging, then roll back, before you go near production. If you have never executed the rollback, you do not have one — you have an intention.

## Make the first production deploy boring

Aim for the deployment to be the least interesting event of the engagement. Everything surprising should already have happened in staging, in week two, when there was time.
lessons.codeExample:
# Multi-stage build: dependencies resolved at build time, because the runtime
# environment has no outbound network access. Nothing downloads at startup.
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
# Their standard: non-root, no shell tooling left in the final image.
RUN useradd --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin appuser
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .
USER appuser

# Every environment-specific value is injected, never baked. The same image
# runs on a laptop and in their production, differing only by these.
ENV APP_DB_URL="" \
    APP_MODEL_ENDPOINT="" \
    APP_LOG_LEVEL=INFO

EXPOSE 8000

# Liveness: is the process alive? Restart if not.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request;urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health')"

# /ready is separate and checked by the load balancer, not by Docker: it
# verifies the database is reachable and migrations are applied. An instance
# that is healthy but not ready must NOT receive traffic.
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
keyTakeaways: Their base images, registries, networks and change windows are constraints, not preferences
One artifact, configuration injected — test by repointing it with an environment variable
Health and readiness are different checks; conflating them routes traffic to instances that cannot serve
Assume no outbound network: bake in or mount anything you would otherwise download
Rehearse the rollback in staging, or you do not have one

questions.prompt: Why must health and readiness be separate checks?
questions.explanation: A process can be alive but unable to serve — migrations pending, database unreachable. Routing traffic to it produces errors that look like an outage.

options.text: A process can be alive but unable to serve; routing traffic to it causes errors
Because orchestrators require exactly two endpoints
Readiness is a faster check than health
Health checks are for developers and readiness for operators

questions.prompt: The customer's production network has no outbound internet access. What does this most affect?
questions.explanation: Anything resolved at startup — package installs, model weights, remote config — will fail. It must be baked into the image or mounted.

options.text: Anything downloaded at container startup must instead be baked in or mounted
Only the ability to send telemetry
Nothing, since containers are self-contained by definition
Only the container registry pull

modules.title: Operating and Handing Over
modules.summary: Making the system legible to the people who will own it after you leave.

lessons.title: Observability for Someone Else's Operations Team
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Instrument for the person who will be woken up

Your logs are not for you. They are for an operator at 3 a.m. who has never read the code, does not know your abstractions, and needs to decide in five minutes whether this is their problem.

Write every error message so that person can act on it. "Validation failed" tells them nothing. "Rejected 412 of 1,000 rows from the nightly customer export: unparseable renewal_date. Source file: customers-2026-09-19.csv" tells them what happened, how big it is, and who to call.

## Three signals earn their place

For a field deployment, instrument:

- **Did the pipeline run?** A job that silently stops running is the most common and least detected failure of all. Alert on *absence*, not only on errors.
- **Did the volume look normal?** Compare against a trailing median. A load at 30% of typical is a failure wearing a success costume.
- **Is the rejection rate stable?** A jump means the source changed.

Everything else is nice to have. These three catch most of what actually goes wrong.

## Correlate across the request

Give every ingest run and every user request an id, put it in every log line and return it in error responses. When the customer reports a problem, they quote the id and you find the whole story in one query.

Without this you are grepping by timestamp across three services, which is a twenty-minute job that should be a ten-second one.

## A runbook, not a diagram

Architecture diagrams are for the design review. What operations needs is a page per alert: what it means, how to check, what to do, who to escalate to.

If you write one artifact at handover, write this one.

## Alert on what needs a human

Every alert that does not require action trains the team to ignore alerts — including the one that matters. Be ruthless: if nobody would do anything at 3 a.m., it is a dashboard metric, not an alert.
lessons.codeExample:
import logging, uuid, statistics

log = logging.getLogger("ingest")

def run_ingest(source, conn):
    run_id = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]   # quoted by the customer, found in one query
    log.info("ingest.start run_id=%s source=%s", run_id, source.name)

    result = load(source.rows(), conn)

    # Signal 2: volume against the trailing median. A load at 30% of normal is a
    # failure wearing a success costume, and nothing else will catch it.
    history = conn.fetch_scalars(
        "SELECT rows_accepted FROM ingest_audit "
        "WHERE source = %s ORDER BY load_date DESC LIMIT 14", (source.name,))
    if history:
        median = statistics.median(history)
        if median and result.accepted < median * 0.6:
            log.error(
                "ingest.volume_low run_id=%s source=%s accepted=%d median_14d=%.0f "
                "ACTION: check whether the upstream export completed; do not publish "
                "today's report until confirmed. Escalate to: data-platform on-call.",
                run_id, source.name, result.accepted, median)

    # Signal 3: rejection rate. A jump means the source changed under us.
    rate = len(result.rejected) / result.read if result.read else 0
    if rate > 0.05:
        top = collections.Counter(r for _, r in result.rejected).most_common(1)[0]
        log.error(
            "ingest.reject_rate_high run_id=%s source=%s rate=%.1f%% top_reason=%r (%d rows) "
            "ACTION: compare today's file header against docs/source-contract.md — "
            "this usually means a column changed. Runbook: docs/runbook.md#reject-rate",
            run_id, source.name, rate * 100, top[0], top[1])

    conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO ingest_audit (run_id, source, rows_read, rows_accepted, rows_rejected) "
        "VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s)",
        (run_id, source.name, result.read, result.accepted, len(result.rejected)))

    # Signal 1 is the absence of this line. A separate watchdog alerts when no
    # successful run has been recorded in 26 hours — silent stoppage is the
    # most common failure and the least likely to be noticed.
    log.info("ingest.done run_id=%s read=%d accepted=%d rejected=%d",
             run_id, result.read, result.accepted, len(result.rejected))
    return result
keyTakeaways: Write errors for a 3 a.m. operator who has never read the code
Alert on absence of a run, not only on failures — silent stoppage is the commonest failure
Compare load volume against a trailing median; an undersized load is a failure in disguise
Thread a correlation id through every log line and error response
Ship a runbook page per alert; and delete any alert nobody would act on

questions.prompt: Why alert on the absence of a successful run rather than only on errors?
questions.explanation: A job that stops being scheduled produces no errors at all. Error-only alerting is blind to the most common silent failure.

options.text: A job that silently stops running produces no errors to alert on
Absence alerts are cheaper to compute
Error alerts are unreliable in containers
It satisfies audit requirements

questions.prompt: What makes an error message useful to an operator who has never read the code?
questions.explanation: Scale, source and next action let someone decide in five minutes whether it is theirs. A category name alone does not.

options.text: It states what happened, at what scale, in which source, and what to do next
It includes the full stack trace and nothing else
It names the class and method that raised it
It is short enough to fit on one line

lessons.title: Handover That Survives Your Departure
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The real deliverable is their capability

Six months after you leave, one of two things is true. Either the customer's own people are changing, running and trusting the system, or it has quietly stopped being used and nobody wants to say so.

Which one happens is decided by how you spent the last two weeks, not the first two.

## Teach by making them drive

Do not demo the deployment process. Sit next to someone while *they* do it, with you answering questions. Then have them do it again with you in the room but silent. Then have them do it without you.

Three repetitions, escalating independence. This takes half a day and is the single highest-return activity of the engagement.

## Hand over the failure paths, not the happy path

Anyone can run the working case. What they need from you is the broken ones: what the three most likely failures look like, how to tell them apart, and what to do about each.

Cause one deliberately in front of them. A team that has seen the alert fire and followed the runbook once will handle it at 3 a.m.; a team that has only read about it will call you.

## Document the decisions, not the code

The code says what it does. What disappears when you leave is *why*: why the risk threshold is 0.6, why usage is weighted below contract terms, why the previous churn tool failed and what that constrains.

A short decisions file is worth more than extensive API documentation, because the API documentation can be regenerated and the reasoning cannot.

## Name an owner, in writing

A system owned by "the team" is owned by nobody. Get a name against it before you leave, and make sure that person has been through the three repetitions.

## Agree how success gets measured after you go

You set a baseline in week one. Agree who re-measures it, and when. Without that, the question of whether this worked becomes a matter of opinion, and opinion drifts toward whoever is loudest.
keyTakeaways: The deliverable is the customer's capability, not the running system
Teach by three escalating repetitions until they can deploy without you
Rehearse the failure paths deliberately; the happy path teaches nothing
Document decisions and their reasons — code cannot regenerate why
Name an individual owner and agree who re-measures the baseline, and when

questions.prompt: What is the most effective way to hand over operational knowledge?
questions.explanation: Escalating repetitions build actual capability. Watching a demo produces recognition, not competence.

options.text: Have them perform the operation three times with decreasing help from you
Demo the process carefully while they take notes
Record a video walkthrough they can rewatch
Write thorough step-by-step documentation

questions.prompt: Why document decisions rather than the code itself?
questions.explanation: Why the threshold is 0.6, and what previous attempt constrained it, exists only in your head. The code's behaviour can always be re-read.

options.text: The reasoning behind a choice cannot be recovered from the code; the behaviour can
Code documentation is always auto-generated

modules.title: LLM Features That Hold Up
modules.summary: Where a model earns its place in a workflow, and how to make its output trustworthy.

lessons.title: Where an LLM Actually Helps a Customer Workflow
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The question is not "can we use AI here"

You will be asked to. The useful question is narrower: *which step in this workflow is slow because a human is reading unstructured text, and what happens if the answer is occasionally wrong?*

Those two dimensions — unstructured input, tolerable error — decide almost everything.

## Where models earn their place

- **Reading long documents to find a specific thing.** The analyst who Ctrl-Fs a contract for a notice period is doing work a model does well, and the answer is checkable against the quoted clause.
- **Normalising messy free text into structure.** Support tickets into categories, notes into fields. Errors are visible and correctable.
- **Drafting something a human will edit.** A first draft that is 80% right saves real time because the human is already reviewing.

The common thread: the human stays in the loop and can see the evidence.

## Where they do not

- **Arithmetic and aggregation.** If the answer is a sum, compute it. A model that usually gets the total right is worse than useless, because the failures are silent and plausible.
- **Decisions with no review step.** Anything that acts without a human seeing it needs a much higher bar than a two-week engagement can establish.
- **Things a rule handles.** If the logic is "flag accounts where usage dropped 40% and renewal is inside 60 days", that is a WHERE clause. It is faster, free, explainable and correct.

That last one is the most common mistake in the field, and resisting it is a large part of your value.

## Deterministic core, model at the edges

The pattern that survives: compute the facts deterministically, and use the model to explain, summarise or extract — never to calculate.

In a renewal copilot, the risk score is arithmetic on usage and contract data. The model explains what the contract says about notice periods and cites the clause. Ask the model for the score and you have built something you cannot defend when the customer asks why an account moved.

flowchart LR A[(Usage + contract data)] --> B[Deterministic risk score
pure functions, tested] B --> C[Ranked account list] D[(Contract text)] --> E[Retrieval] E --> F[LLM: explain + cite clause] C --> G[Analyst review] F --> G B -.->|never ask the model
for the number| F
keyTakeaways: Ask which step is slow because a human reads unstructured text, and what a wrong answer costs
Models earn their place on document search, text-to-structure and reviewable drafts
Never use a model for arithmetic — silent plausible failures are the worst kind
If a rule expresses the logic, write the rule; it is faster, free and explainable
Deterministic core, model at the edges: compute facts, generate explanations

lessons.title: Grounding, Citations and Refusal
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Trust is lost once

The renewals team in our worked example abandoned a previous tool because "it gave us a number with no reason attached". That is the normal outcome. A tool that is confidently wrong twice in front of a sceptical user is finished, and no amount of subsequent accuracy recovers it.

So the design constraint comes first: every statement the system makes about the customer's documents must be traceable to a passage in those documents, shown alongside the claim.

## Retrieve, then constrain

Ground the answer in retrieved passages and instruct the model to use nothing else. Pass the passages with identifiers, require the identifier in the output, and validate that the identifier it cited actually exists before showing anything.

That last check matters. A model will occasionally cite a passage id that was never in the context, and an unvalidated citation is worse than none — it looks like evidence.

## Make refusal a first-class output

The system must be able to say *"the contract does not address this"*. Design the response shape so refusal is a normal value rather than a failure, and make refusing cheap and unremarkable in the prompt.

If the only way to satisfy the output format is to produce an answer, the model will produce one.

## Show the passage, not just a link

Quote the text inline. The reviewer should be able to judge the claim without navigating anywhere. A footnote reference that requires a click is a footnote nobody checks, and unchecked citations are decoration.

## Test the refusal path hardest

Your evaluation set needs questions the documents genuinely cannot answer, and the system must refuse all of them. This is the test people skip, and it is the one that predicts whether the tool survives contact with real users.
keyTakeaways: A tool that is confidently wrong twice in front of users does not recover
Every claim must carry the passage it came from, quoted inline
Validate that cited identifiers actually existed in the context before displaying
Make refusal a normal, cheap output — otherwise the format forces an answer
Test unanswerable questions hardest; refusal quality predicts survival

questions.prompt: Why validate that a cited passage identifier appeared in the supplied context?
questions.explanation: Models occasionally cite identifiers that were never provided. An unvalidated citation looks like evidence while being fabricated — worse than showing none.

options.text: Models sometimes cite identifiers that were never in the context, and a fake citation looks like evidence
To keep the context window small
To reduce token cost
Because identifiers must be sequential

questions.prompt: Why must refusal be an explicitly supported output shape?
questions.explanation: If every valid response requires an answer, the format itself pressures the model into inventing one. Refusal has to be cheap and normal.

options.text: If the output format requires an answer, the model will produce one rather than refuse
Because refusals are cheaper to generate
Because regulators require a refusal path
Because users prefer short responses

modules.title: Evaluation Before Confidence
modules.summary: Measuring quality with the customer's own examples, and knowing the cost and latency numbers before you are asked for them.

lessons.title: Building an Eval Set From the Customer's Own Examples
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Their examples, not yours

Generic benchmarks tell you nothing about whether this works here. What matters is the customer's own hard cases: the contract with the unusual notice clause, the account that everyone agrees is at risk for a reason the data does not show, the question that has three defensible answers.

Collect these during discovery. Ask directly: *"Give me ten cases where this is hard, and tell me the right answer for each."* You will get better test data in an hour than you could construct in a week, and the act of collecting it is itself discovery.

## Include the unanswerable

At least a quarter of the set should be questions the documents genuinely do not address. The system must refuse every one.

Without these, you are measuring only how well it answers, which is exactly the half that fails safely. The dangerous failure is the confident answer to a question with no basis.

## Run it on every change

An eval set that runs on demand is an eval set that stops being run. Put it in CI. When a prompt change improves one case and breaks two, you want to know in three minutes, not at the demo.

Prompt changes are unusually prone to this: they feel local and behave globally.

## Score what the customer cares about

For a grounded question-answering system, three numbers:

- **Correct with a valid citation** — the only fully good outcome.
- **Refused** — good when the answer is not in the documents, bad when it is.
- **Answered without valid grounding** — the one that must be zero.

Report these separately. A single accuracy percentage hides the distinction between a system that is cautious and one that is dangerous.

## Show the customer the failures

Walk them through the cases that fail. This is counterintuitive and it works: a customer who has seen the honest failure profile trusts the successes, and they will often tell you that two of the five failures do not matter and one of them matters enormously. That is information you cannot get any other way.
lessons.codeExample:
# evals/test_grounded_answers.py — runs in CI on every change to a prompt.
import json, pytest
from app.grounding import ask

CASES = json.load(open("evals/customer_cases.json"))
# Collected with the renewals team in week 1. 40 cases: 28 answerable from the
# contracts, 12 deliberately not. Their answers, not ours.

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", [c for c in CASES if c["answerable"]],
                         ids=lambda c: c["id"])
def test_answerable(case, client, clauses_for):
    got = ask(case["question"], clauses_for(case["contract"]), client)
    assert got.answer is not None, f"refused an answerable question: {case['question']}"
    assert got.clause_id == case["expected_clause"], (
        f"cited {got.clause_id}, expected {case['expected_clause']}")

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", [c for c in CASES if not c["answerable"]],
                         ids=lambda c: c["id"])
def test_unanswerable_is_refused(case, client, clauses_for):
    got = ask(case["question"], clauses_for(case["contract"]), client)
    # The failure that ends deployments: a confident answer with no basis.
    assert got.answer is None, (
        f"answered an unanswerable question: {case['question']!r} -> {got.answer!r}")

def test_report(client, clauses_for, record_property):
    """Three numbers, reported separately. A single accuracy figure would hide
    the difference between a cautious system and a dangerous one."""
    correct = refused = ungrounded = 0
    for case in CASES:
        got = ask(case["question"], clauses_for(case["contract"]), client)
        if got.answer is None:
            refused += 1
        elif got.clause_id == case["expected_clause"]:
            correct += 1
        else:
            ungrounded += 1

    record_property("correct_with_citation", correct)
    record_property("refused", refused)
    record_property("answered_without_valid_grounding", ungrounded)
    assert ungrounded == 0, f"{ungrounded} answers had no valid grounding"
keyTakeaways: Collect hard cases from the customer during discovery, with their correct answers
A quarter of the set should be unanswerable; the system must refuse all of them
Run evals in CI — prompt changes feel local and behave globally
Report correct-with-citation, refused and ungrounded-answer separately; the last must be zero
Show the customer the failures; it builds trust and reprioritises the work

questions.prompt: Why must an evaluation set include questions the documents cannot answer?
questions.explanation: Answerable-only evaluation measures the half that fails safely. The dangerous failure is a confident answer with no basis, and only unanswerable cases detect it.

options.text: Without them you only measure answering, and miss confident answers with no basis
To increase the size of the test set
Because refusals are faster to evaluate
To satisfy the customer's compliance team

questions.prompt: Why report correct, refused and ungrounded separately rather than one accuracy figure?
questions.explanation: One number cannot distinguish a cautious system from a dangerous one — both can score identically while failing in opposite directions.

options.text: A single figure cannot distinguish an over-cautious system from a dangerous one
Because accuracy is hard to compute
Because customers prefer more metrics
Because refusals should not count as failures in any context

lessons.title: Cost, Latency and the Numbers You Will Be Asked For
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## You will be asked, and "it depends" is not an answer

At some point — usually in front of someone senior — you will be asked what this costs to run. Arrive with a number, its basis, and the assumption that moves it most.

> *"About \$340 a month at the current volume: roughly 1,200 reviews, averaging 8,000 input and 400 output tokens. The input side dominates, so retrieving fewer passages is the lever. Halving retrieved context takes it to about \$200."*

That answer ends the conversation constructively. "It depends on usage" starts a worse one.

## Measure per unit of work, not per call

A single review may involve several model calls. The customer does not think in calls; they think in reviews. Instrument at the level of the user's unit of work and you can quote a cost per review, which is the number that can be compared to the time it saves.

## Input tokens usually dominate

In a retrieval system, the retrieved context is typically far larger than the question or the answer. That means your cost lever is retrieval: how many passages, how large, and whether they are needed.

Halving retrieved passages often halves cost and sometimes improves accuracy, because there is less irrelevant material to be distracted by. Measure both when you change it — the eval set exists for exactly this.

## Latency is a workflow property

Two seconds is fine when the analyst is reading the previous answer. Two seconds is not fine when it blocks a list from rendering. Ask where in the workflow the wait lands before optimising anything.

Often the best latency work is not making the call faster but moving it: precompute the nightly ranking, and the interactive path only pays for the one question the user actually asks.

## Log usage from the first day

Token counts per request, with the correlation id. Retrofitting this is tedious and you will want the history the first time someone asks whether costs are growing.
lessons.codeExample:
# Cost per REVIEW, not per call. A review is what the customer thinks in, and
# it is the number that can be weighed against the 20 minutes it saves them.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

PRICING = {  # USD per 1M tokens — confirm against current provider pricing
    "input": 3.00,
    "output": 15.00,
}

@dataclass
class ReviewUsage:
    review_id: str
    calls: list = field(default_factory=list)      # (purpose, in_tokens, out_tokens)

    def record(self, purpose, usage):
        self.calls.append((purpose, usage.input_tokens, usage.output_tokens))

    def cost_usd(self) -> float:
        tin = sum(c[1] for c in self.calls)
        tout = sum(c[2] for c in self.calls)
        return tin / 1e6 * PRICING["input"] + tout / 1e6 * PRICING["output"]

    def breakdown(self) -> str:
        """Which call dominates. Almost always the one carrying retrieved context."""
        lines = []
        for purpose, tin, tout in sorted(self.calls, key=lambda c: -c[1]):
            share = tin / 1e6 * PRICING["input"] + tout / 1e6 * PRICING["output"]
            lines.append(f"  {purpose:<24} in={tin:>6} out={tout:>5}  ${share:.4f}")
        return "\n".join(lines)


# Example output after one review:
#   clause_qa (6 passages)     in=  8140 out=  380  $0.0301
#   summarise_usage            in=   920 out=  210  $0.0059
#   -> $0.036 per review; at 1,200 reviews/month = $43/month
#
# The lever is visible: clause_qa carries the retrieved passages and is 84% of
# the cost. Dropping from 6 passages to 3 was tested against the eval set —
# cost fell to $0.019 and correct-with-citation was unchanged at 26/28.
keyTakeaways: Arrive with a cost figure, its basis and the assumption that moves it most
Measure cost per unit of the user's work, not per model call
Retrieved context usually dominates input cost — retrieval is the main lever
Fewer passages can cut cost and improve accuracy; measure both against the eval set
Latency matters where it lands in the workflow; often the fix is precomputation, not speed

lessons.title: Turning Field Evidence Into Product Requirements
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The half of the job that is easy to skip

You are busy, the customer is happy, the engagement is ending. Writing up what you learned feels like overhead.

It is the difference between a field engineer and an expensive contractor. The company is paying field rates partly to learn what it cannot learn from a dashboard, and you are the only channel.

## Count before you recommend

"Customers keep struggling with X" is an anecdote and will be treated as one. "Four of the last six deployments needed a custom connector for the same class of source system, costing eleven engineer-days total" is a requirement with a business case attached.

Keep a running tally across engagements. The pattern that justifies a product change is almost never visible inside one deployment.

## Separate the one-off from the recurring

Some of what you build genuinely belongs to one customer: their org chart, their peculiar approval flow. Some of it is the same thing you built last time with different field names.

The second category is the product's backlog, and you are the only person positioned to tell them apart. Be honest about it — arguing that a bespoke thing should be productised because you enjoyed building it wastes everyone's time.

## Bring the artifact, not just the story

Product teams act on evidence they can hold: the actual connector code, the discovery log, the eval case that fails, the customer's words verbatim. Three real quotes from three customers saying the same thing moves a roadmap. A summary of your impression does not.

## Say what it cost

Frame in engineering days. "This gap cost eleven days across four deployments, and will cost roughly three days per future deployment" is a sentence a product manager can prioritise against. "This is painful" is not.

## Accept when the answer is no

Sometimes the product team will decline, correctly, because your four customers are not representative. Take it, log it, and raise it again when the count is twelve. Being the person who reports reality rather than lobbying for it is what makes you believed the next time.
lessons.codeExample:
# field-report/2026-09-renewals.md

## Pattern: nightly CSV sources with drifting schemas
Seen in 4 of the last 6 deployments (Acme, Northwind, Contoso, Fabrikam).

### Evidence
| Deployment | Custom connector? | Days spent | Drift incidents in first 90d |
|------------|-------------------|-----------:|-----------------------------:|
| Acme       | yes               |        3.0 |                            2 |
| Northwind  | yes               |        2.5 |                            1 |
| Contoso    | yes               |        3.5 |                            4 |
| Fabrikam   | yes               |        2.0 |                            1 |
| **Total**  |                   |   **11.0** |                        **8** |

### What we built four times
The same three things with different field names: drift detection against a
declared contract, rejected-row retention with reasons, and an idempotent
upsert on a natural key. Attached: the four connectors, diffed — 68% identical.

### Customer words (verbatim)
- Acme, data lead: "We can't promise the export won't change. Nobody owns it."
- Contoso, ops:    "It stopped using the region field for a month and we only
                    found out because a report looked odd."
- Northwind, IT:   "Every vendor asks us to fix the export. None of them do."

### Recommendation
A declarative source-contract feature in the product: declare expected columns
and types, get drift detection, rejection retention and reconciliation for free.

### Cost of not doing it
~11 engineer-days already spent; ~3 days per future deployment of this shape,
which is roughly two thirds of the pipeline we are currently selling into.

### What would change my mind
If the next three deployments are API-based rather than file-based, this is a
shrinking problem and should not be built. Re-check at six more deployments.
keyTakeaways: Field learning is the reason the company pays field rates; writing it up is the job
Count across engagements — the pattern is rarely visible inside one deployment
Distinguish genuinely bespoke work from the thing you have now built three times
Bring artifacts and verbatim customer words, not impressions
Frame in engineering days saved; accept a no and re-raise with a larger count

lessons.title: The Forward Deployed Interview
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What they are actually testing

Forward deployed interviews are unusual: the coding bar is real but rarely the deciding factor. What is being tested is whether you can be trusted alone in front of a customer.

Concretely, four things:

1. **Do you find the real problem, or build what you are told?**
2. **What do you do when the customer is wrong?**
3. **Can you make progress with incomplete information?**
4. **Do you tell the truth when it is inconvenient?**

## Have three stories ready

For each: a deployment that went well, one that went badly, and one where you changed the customer's mind. Rehearse them to about two minutes each.

The failure story carries the most weight. Choose a real one, name what you missed, and say what you now do differently. A candidate with no failure story has either not deployed anything or is not being straight, and interviewers for this role are unusually good at detecting the second.

## Expect the ambiguous scenario

You will get something like: *"The customer says they need a dashboard. After two days you believe a dashboard will not help. What do you do?"*

They are not looking for a clever answer. They want to hear you gather evidence, show it rather than argue it, offer an alternative, and — crucially — accept that they may still want the dashboard and that it is their business.

The failure mode they are screening for is the engineer who is right and ignored.

## The coding round is about pragmatism

Expect messy data and an ambiguous requirement rather than an algorithm puzzle. Ask clarifying questions out loud — that *is* part of the test. Handle the malformed input. Say what you would do with more time.

Perfect code that ignored the ambiguity scores worse than working code that named it.

## Ask what their deployments actually look like

How long is a typical engagement? How much of what gets built is bespoke? What happens to field feedback? How often does the field team say no to a customer?

The last one tells you the most. A company where the field team can never say no is a company where you will be underwater by month three.
keyTakeaways: The bar is whether you can be trusted alone with a customer, not raw coding speed
Prepare three two-minute stories: success, failure, and changing a customer's mind
For ambiguous scenarios: gather evidence, show it, offer an alternative, accept their call
In the coding round, ask clarifying questions aloud and handle the messy input
Ask how often their field team says no to a customer — the answer predicts your workload
